---
title: "Specific Heat near the Lambda Transition"
source_chapter: "10"
source_section: "10.6.4"
source_page: 292
---

> [!TLDR]
> The helium-4 lambda transition has a sharp but finite heat-capacity cusp because its critical exponent α is slightly negative.

The apparent puzzle is that a sharp peak can remain finite while its slope becomes singular. Separate the regular background from the singular correction before interpreting the graph. The power law is an asymptotic equilibrium description close to the lambda point, with a specified heat-capacity normalization and the same control conditions on each side.

Near a continuous transition, the singular part of the heat capacity follows a power law:

$$
{\thermal{C}}_{\mathrm{sing}}\sim A_\pm |t|^{-\alpha},\qquad t=\frac{{\thermal{T}}-{\thermal{T}}_c}{{\thermal{T}}_c}.
$$

The amplitudes above and below the transition can differ. The exponent determines the limiting behavior:

- $\alpha>0$: a power-law divergence.
- $\alpha=0$: a logarithmic divergence can occur, or a finite jump in a mean-field model.
- $\alpha<0$: the singular contribution tends to zero. A regular background can produce a finite cusp.

For the helium-4 lambda transition, the source gives $\alpha\approx-0.013$. Thus the heat capacity has a finite, very sharp cusp, rather than an infinite value.

**Fig. 10.4** Finite heat-capacity cusp at the helium-4 lambda transition. The illustrative curves use ${\thermal{C}}={\thermal{C}}_c-A_\pm|t|^{0.013}$ with a constant regular background and a larger amplitude above the transition ($A_+>A_-$), so the heat capacity is larger below ${\thermal{T}}_\lambda$, as measured for helium-4. The axes have no absolute heat-capacity scale. The curve reaches the finite value ${\thermal{C}}_c$ at ${\thermal{T}}={\thermal{T}}_\lambda$. Its slope becomes singular.

> [!warning] Source correction — finite cusp
> The source sketch labels the peak as a divergence. For its stated helium-4 exponent $\alpha\approx-0.013$, the heat capacity stays finite. The new figure shows this finite cusp. A positive exponent would instead give a divergent heat capacity.

The amplitude ratio is universal within a universality class when the same definitions and limits are used. Individual amplitudes depend on the material. See [[10.07.03 Universality and Universality Classes]].

With the source's negative exponent, the singular correction vanishes on approach to the transition, but its derivative contains a negative power of the reduced-temperature magnitude. Thus a finite limiting heat capacity and an unbounded slope are compatible. The schematic graph chooses the signs of the amplitudes to show a peak; the exponent alone does not determine every background or amplitude.

For an independent empirical reference, [Lipa and co-workers report heat-capacity measurements in orbit](https://arxiv.org/abs/cond-mat/0310163), where reduced gravitational pressure gradients limited one source of rounding. This is evidence from a separate experiment, not a measurement represented by the illustrative graph. The source exponent and graph values above are retained. Comparing fitted singular terms requires control of background subtraction, temperature resolution, and rounding.

## Physical quantities

| Symbol | Unit | Quantity | Description |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| $A_\pm$ | $\unit{J\,K^{-1}}$ | Heat-capacity amplitudes | Coefficients of the reduced-temperature singular term on each side. |
| ${\thermal{T}}_\lambda$ | $\unit{K}$ | Lambda temperature | Transition temperature of liquid helium-4. |
| ${\thermal{C}}$ | $\unit{J\,K^{-1}}$ | Heat capacity | Total heat capacity under the stated constraint. |
| ${\thermal{T}}$ | $\unit{K}$ | Temperature | Absolute temperature of the system. |
| ${\thermal{T}}_c$ | $\unit{K}$ | Critical temperature | Temperature of the stated phase transition. |
